title: Progressive Hangovers
author: Samuel Sadler
summary: Samuel Sadler argues that the classical Christian school movement, for all its progress, is still carrying inherited progressive assumptions that it should deliberately shed. He frames the acronym soup of classical organizations as different answers to what was lost, which he identifies as paideia, and notes there is no single answer to which curriculum and methods are most faithful to it. The first generation of classical educators came from progressive schools and bolted Socratic discussion and the trivium stages onto an existing progressive model, which he honors but says must be moved past. His main target is the standard school day, with its uniform block schedule, which he contrasts with Calvin's Geneva, Luther's two-hour plan, one-room schools and private tutors. He argues that progressive education treats all students alike and tends toward the lowest common denominator, while the Western Christian paideia accepts unequal strengths and diverse formation. He closes by welcoming experiments such as co-ops, university-model and single-sex schools and urging diversity of models.
points: The author names paideia as what classical educators are trying to recover, and argues no single curriculum or method settles how to do it faithfully.
Early classical schools often added Socratic seminars and trivium stages onto a progressive school structure, which is a starting point but not the destination.
The uniform block-schedule school day is presented as the clearest progressive hangover, since it limits teachers' freedom to draw out strengths and target weaknesses.
Historical models such as Luther's brief daily plan, one-room schools and private tutoring show that varied structures have long served liberal education.
Co-ops, university-model, Charlotte Mason, single-sex and forest schools are encouraged as experiments, with diversity of models as the guiding principle.
quotes: Without the anchor of the past, progressive education became a shapeshifting organism whose goals, methods, and metrics exist in a constant state of flux. And for a while, this organism had a monopoly on education in America.
With a limited number of guiding texts, classical ed meant things like socratic discussion, grammar-stage-logic-stage-rhetoric-stage, and teaching how to think instead of what to think.
However, these implementations were added as modifications to the existing school model… a largely progressive model.
At the risk of generalization, progressive education assumes that the same education is fit for all. It is a leveler which, unfortunately, tends toward the lowest common denominator.
The top third are frequently bored, the bottom third are overwhelmed, and the middle third are somewhere in between, depending on the day.

Classical educators are already experimenting with new structures for the school day: there exist already classical co-ops, in person or online, university-model schools, Charlotte Mason schools, single-sex schools or classrooms, forest schools, and go-live-on-a-farm schools.

In one sense, tailoring education to individual needs is a very progressive idea. However, what the classical tradition knows, which progressives lost, is that many of the individual’s needs are met by tradition and the liberal arts.
